transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-24 15:00 PST | Duration 42m | Redwood: Alex, Priya, Jordan | Solarflare: Marta, Ethan, Raj, Nina

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex Rivera from Redwood Inference, AE on this account. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer, and Jordan from customer success. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Marta: Hi Alex, doing well, thanks. Marta here. We're excited to see the hosted API walkthrough.
[00:12] Raj: Raj here, we'll keep this pretty technical, Ethan will field most of the ML questions.
[00:16] Alex: Great. Quick agenda - we'll show a short demo of hosted chat/text generation basics, covering streaming, key params (temp/top_p/max_tokens/stop), retries & error handling, and a quick look at the Redwood Console for observability. We'll leave time for questions and next steps. Sound good?
[00:27] Ethan: Sounds good.
[00:28] Priya: I'll share my screen now — sorry if there's a slight lag.
[00:35] (screen share starts)
[00:40] Priya: Okay, pulled up the demo app and the SDK snippet. This is a simple chat example using the hosted API, calling /v1/chat/completions. We set streaming=true for low-latency partial responses. If you see the terminal, you can see tokens emitted as they arrive.
[00:55] Ethan: Nice, does streaming reduce overall cost or just perceived latency?
[01:00] Priya: Mostly perceived latency — you get tokens as they are generated. Cost is per-token regardless, but streaming lets UI show progressive results and reduces time-to-first-byte. For some use cases you can stop earlier (using stop sequences) and save tokens.
[01:15] Marta: Ok, and how do you handle retries if a transient GPU error occurs? We need something robust for customer-facing chat.
[01:22] Priya: Good question. The hosted API has built-in retry guidance — the SDK exposes retryable errors and we recommend exponential backoff with jitter. The server implements idempotency keys for requests where you want exactly-once semantics for a session state update. For streaming requests you can resume with the last good token index in some cases, but typically you'd replay idempotent messages.
[01:45] Raj: Are there automatic rate-limit headers so we can do client-side backoff?
[01:49] Priya: Yes — rate-limit and capacity headers are returned. We also surface per-key quotas in the Console so platform teams can automate backoff.
[01:57] Ethan: How about parameters — what's the tradeoff between temperature and top_p? Any defaults you recommend?
[02:03] Priya: Defaults are conservative, like temp 0.2 and top_p 0.9 for assistant-style answers. Temp controls randomness, top_p controls nucleus sampling. For deterministic generation (legal docs, etc.) we'd push temp closer to 0 and tighten top_p. For creative copy you can increase. Also watch max_tokens — it directly affects cost, so set a reasonable max and use stop sequences.
[02:28] Alex: Quick note — Optimize can suggest parameter profiles based on your dataset and quality targets. We'll share a sample Optimize report after the call.
[02:36] Marta: That would be useful.
[02:38] Priya: Switching to the Console — here's the route dashboard. You get token-level cost, latency percentiles, error rates, and model breakdowns. You can also set canary rollouts per model version.
[02:50] (short pause as console loads)
[03:00] Priya: See this trace — it shows a request that used prefix caching; prefix or KV cache hits reduce inference time significantly for chat-like workloads.
[03:10] Ethan: When does the KV cache persist? Is it per-session or across sessions?
[03:14] Priya: It's configurable. For hosted we support session-scoped caches to avoid leakage across users; enterprise/dedicated customers can opt for longer-lived caches if they trust the data residency model.
[03:28] Nina: On residency — we have to keep PII in our VPC and control keys. What options do you have for key management and private deployments?
[03:36] Alex: For enterprise we offer Redwood Private — VPC connectors and on-prem packages. For hosted we integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest and we support bring-your-own-key in dedicated contexts. We'll send the security pack with SOC 2, ISO binder, and KMS details.
[03:54] Nina: Great. Please include audit log retention options. That's key for our compliance team.
[03:58] Alex: Absolutely.
[04:00] Priya: Back to retries — another pattern is async completion: submit job, poll for result. That avoids streaming complexity if you need guaranteed completion at expense of latency. We also support webhook callbacks for job-ready events.
[04:16] Ethan: For webhooks, how do you manage duplicate deliveries? We need idempotency.
[04:20] Priya: Webhooks include delivery IDs and you can use idempotency keys. We also provide SDK helpers to dedupe.
[04:27] Alex: A common architecture we see is hosted for initial velocity and then move to dedicated pools once predictable throughput is reached. Dedicated offers reserved capacity and lower tail latency SLAs.
[04:39] Raj: What's the break-even from cost perspective — any rule of thumb?
[04:43] Priya: It depends on concurrency and token volume. For sustained, predictable high throughput (tens of thousands tokens/day with high concurrency) dedicated is usually more economical. We'll run numbers for your 50k tokens/day profile in the benchmark worksheet.
[04:58] Marta: How do you measure latency SLOs? 95th and 99th percentiles?
[05:03] Priya: We surface p50/p95/p99 and tail latencies per model and route. Console allows alerts on those and automatic fallback policies to cheaper variants if SLAs are at risk.
[05:18] Ethan: Any tools to tune batching? Our traffic has spikes with chat sessions.
[05:23] Priya: Yes — the runtime supports continuous batching and you can configure batching windows. Optimize offers suggestions for batch sizes and quantization profiles to balance latency and cost.
[05:34] (Priya scrolls)
[05:36] Priya: Now a quick live example of parameter changes. I'll set temp to 0.8 and top_p to 0.95 and stream the response. You'll see more creative output and slightly different token timing.
[05:46] (demo runs)
[06:10] Marta: I can already see the tone shift, nice.
[06:12] Ethan: What about retries for streaming mid-response? If connection drops mid-stream, do you re-request?
[06:18] Priya: Good point — typical approach: client buffers last acknowledged token position and retries the request with idempotency key and last user message. If you need seamless UX we sometimes recommend short-lived session caches to resume. It's imperfect in edge cases, so many teams prefer short retransmit logic and reconciling on server side.
[06:38] Alex: Also note network-layer retries should be limited — you don't want to double-bill tokens accidentally; idempotency helps.
[06:45] Raj: On billing, how granular is cost? Per-token? Per-embedding?
[06:49] Alex: Hosted is per-token for generation and per-embedding unit for embeddings. Console shows token breakdown by prompt vs completion. We also provide cost profiles per model so you can route to cheaper variants for lower-priority workloads.
[07:03] Marta: Could you demo a retry scenario? Maybe simulate a transient 5xx?
[07:08] Priya: I can simulate a 502 from the edge. I'll show SDK retry logic - exponential backoff and redeploy of the request with idempotency key.
[07:18] (demo simulates error)
[07:22] Priya: And you can see the SDK logged a retry at 800ms, then succeeded on second try; Console shows a transient spike in error rate but the request completed.
[07:34] Ethan: Nice. Okay, shifting to security: does hosted store logs with raw user content by default? We need to avoid storing PII.
[07:42] Alex: By default we keep minimal logs for troubleshooting; customers can opt-out of storing raw payloads, mask sensitive fields, and configure retention windows. For regulated workloads we recommend dedicated or private deployments with customer-managed storage and encryption.
[07:59] Nina: What's the retention granularity? Days, months?
[08:02] Alex: Configurable — options from 7 days to indefinite for enterprise contracts. We'll include default retention and compliance options in the security pack.
[08:12] Raj: Any mentions of upstream model updates? We want version pinning.
[08:15] Priya: Yes — you can pin model versions and do canary rollouts. Console shows model variants and you can automatically fallback to previous version on regressions. For quality monitoring Optimize ties regressions to prompt sets.
[08:30] Marta: That ties into our QA process. Good.
[08:33] Alex: Quick question for you — what's the most critical success metric for this POC?
[08:38] Marta: Accuracy of answers on our customer support prompts and sub-200ms TTF for short responses.
[08:44] Ethan: Plus cost target — under $0.02 per user session average.
[08:48] Priya: Ok we'll map those targets to test harness. We'll recommend model profiles and batching that meet sub-200ms TTF for single-turn short answers.
[08:58] (short pause)
[09:00] Alex: Any other technical deep dives you'd like in the POC?
[09:04] Raj: We might ask for a private deployment pricing sheet, but initial POC will be hosted. Also want a checklist for SOC2 and SAML setup.
[09:12] Jordan: I'll follow up with the onboarding checklist and link to our SAML docs.
[09:16] Marta: Can you include sample SDK code for Node and Python?
[09:20] Priya: Absolutely. We'll attach snippets and a small quickstart repo.
[09:24] Ethan: One more — do you expose token-level streaming for our analytics pipeline? We want to hook into token events for moderation.
[09:31] Priya: You can stream tokens to client and optionally mirror to webhooks for analytics; be mindful of PII. We also have server-side moderation hooks and content safety models.
[09:41] Nina: Safety models — do you provide filters or integrations with tooling?
[09:45] Priya: We provide built-in safety scoring and you can add custom classifiers in the pipeline. We'll include best-practice docs.
[09:54] Alex: Ok wrapping up demo portion. Quick recap — streaming reduces TTF, use stop sequences to limit tokens, retries via idempotency and exponential backoff, Console shows token and latency breakdowns, Optimize can help tune params and batching.
[10:12] Marta: Thanks, that was helpful.
[10:15] Raj: Next steps?
[10:17] Alex: I'll send pricing and SOC2/security pack; Priya will send benchmark worksheet and SDK snippets; we'll schedule a POC scoping call next week. Also agreed Ethan will share sample prompts and traffic curve.
[10:29] Ethan: I'll upload samples to the share link after this call.
[10:33] Alex: Great — any final questions?
[10:36] Marta: None from me.
[10:37] Nina: No, thanks.
[10:38] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and action items.
[10:43] (call ends)
